item.title: Vuelta a España: Jakob Omrzel wins stage 12 as Enric Mas has another stellar ride on Calar Alto
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: As the Vuelta a España headed back into the mountains and the summit finish at Calar Alto, it was Enric Mas (Movistar) who once again proved the strongest of the GC riders, adding more time to his overall lead with an attack 12km from the finish.Red jersey hopefuls Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) had no answer to Mas' move, with Mas cannily linking up with Movistar teammate from the break, Raúl García Pierna.Gall and Roglič, too, got help from teammates dropping back – Léo Bisiaux and Luke Tuckwell – and a resurgent Gregor Mühlberger. The strength in numbers behind the solo Mas seemingly had no effect, though, with the chasers only losing time as the finish neared.Mas eventually crossed the line with another 27 seconds in the bag, extending his lead over Roglič to 1:45, while Gall now lies at 2:06 down.The GC battle wasn't the fight for stage victory, however. That played out minutes up the road as 20-year-old Vuelta debutant Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) broke clear of what was once a 30-man breakaway group with 11.7km to go. Holding a four-minute lead over Mas and co, he left behind Urko Berrade (Kern Pharma) to go solo to the finish.Omrzel's power was such that even the big GC moves behind barely made a dent in his lead. He hit the final kilometre with a three-minute lead over Mas, and the 2025 Giro Next Gen winner duly converted it to the biggest win of his young career.2024 Vuelta stage winner Berrade crossed the line in second place, 1:56 down, while mountain classification leader Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) took third, 2:13 back. Mas wouldn't add bonus seconds to his total at the line, finishing in sixth, 2:56 down.Omrzel's ride, which saw him in virtual second overall at one point, saw him leap from 10th to sixth overall, 4:59 behind Mas. While the podium trio stayed in place, Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) moved up to third as he finished alongside Gall and Roglič. The Ecuadorian leapfrogged Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos), who dropped away further down the climb to finish 5:05 adrift of Omrzel and 2:09 behind Mas."I'm not surprised because I know how much work I put in, and I knew that these days were going to come sooner or later. But for sure, I was not expecting 100% to do it on my first Grand Tour," Omrzel, who now lies 30 seconds off Onley's white jersey, said after his win."So, I mean, I still can't believe what I did, but I felt super good. I'm still feeling okay. I'm not tired, so I don't know, I'm just enjoying it at the moment."The team behind us is really great. As riders, we understand each other really well, and at the moment, we are working so well together. The whole team is just perfection."We said that we are playing PlayStation, and that's what we are doing at the moment! Whatever we want, we do. We go in the breakaway with Pello [Bilbao], Santi Buitrago], and the other guys. It's just amazing, and I'm really proud of that."After Wednesday's sprint finish in Lorca, the Vuelta a España peloton headed back to the mountains for the 166.6km stage 12 with five classified climbs and 4,500 metres of elevation on the road to Calar Alto (17km at 5.6%).Early third-category ascents including the Alto de Cabecico (8km at 3.3%) and the Alto de Cóbdar (5km at 4.5%) led on to the mid-stage second-category climb, the Collado Garcia (19km at 2.4%). The first-category Alto de Velefique (13km at 7.2%) lay 29km from the line ahead of the stage's final ascent.Georg Steinhauser (EF Education-EasyPost) put in the first major attack of the day, though a solo breakaway on such a tough stage was never likely to stick. More attacks followed after the German was caught, including efforts from João Almeida (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) and points leader Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike).That move, too, was brought back, before Van Aert jumped clear once more on the Alto de Cabecico to grab three mountain points, moving one point nearer to KOM leader Buitrago.It would take some 40km for the breakaway to properly go, as 30 riders jumped clear before the Alto de Cóbdar. Almeida, Van Aert, and Buitrago were up there again. The trio were joined by a host of other notable names, including Mas' teammates Raúl García Pierna and Pablo Castrillo, Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Luke Tuckwell (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Léo Bisiaux (Decathlon CMA CGM), Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech), Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello-Q36.5), Urko Berrade (Kern Pharma), Jack Haig (Netcompany Ineos), Marco Brenner (Tudor), Mauri Vansevenant (Soudal-QuickStep), Alexey Lutsenko (NSN), plus Andreas Leknessund, and Tobias Halland Johannessen (Uno-X Mobility).Omrzel was also in the move, the 20-year-old a GC danger man lying 10th overall at 8:05 down. Movistar and Red Bull lined up at the head of the peloton behind, leaving the break to race over two minutes clear.At the Alto de Cóbdar, the gap was up over four minutes as Van Aert led the race over the top to collect six points to Buitrago's four, moving closer in the mountain classification standings once again.From there, the road kept on gradually rising, stop-start, to the Collado Garcia. Again it was Van Aert vs Buitrago at the top, and again, Van Aert led the way. The Belgian took five points to the Colombian's three, putting him at 30 to 38 in the KOM standings.With 80km and two climbs left to tackle, the break enjoyed a six-minute lead, a gap that reached 7:30 in the valley road – putting Omrzel up to virtual second place overall.Up ahead, Almeida gave his all on the uphill towards the Alto de Velefique as Van Aert grabbed 20 points at the intermediate sprint. The Portuguese rider's effort helped split apart the breakaway group, while further back, race leader Enric Mas was down to a single helper in Iván Romeo, with Castrillo and García Pierna still well up the road.On the climb itself, Carapaz was the first man to make a big attack. The Ecuadorian attacked with 37km to go, 6km from the top, quickly taking a 30-second lead over a GC group which counted only around 15 riders.Up front, 5:30 clear of Mas, Omrzel made a move to go clear. He took Bisiaux with him, the pair taking 20 seconds on the rest of the break. They were brought back a kilometre from the top, however, while further down, Romeo dragged back Carapaz, too.Buitrago led Lutsenko across the summit for another 10 mountain points to go clear of Van Aert once more. They were joined by seven more at the front in Omrzel, Bisiaux, Berrade, Haig, Tuckwell, García Pierna, and Vansevenant.5:30 back, Castrillo had waited for the GC group to help Mas, while García Pierna slowed from the breakaway at the bottom of the climb to provide assistance later on. Romeo and Castrillo led the GC group onto the climb.Buitrago's early acceleration at the front blew the break apart for good, leaving just him, Omrzel, Bisiaux, and Berrade out front. In the GC group, Decathlon took over the pacemaking 15km from the top, quickly dropping Mattias Skjelmose (Lidl-Trek) and Sepp Kuss (Visma-Lease a Bike).Gall launched soon afterwards, taking Mas and Roglič with him as Onley – who suffered a minor crash early in the stage – was dropped along with Carapaz.Buitrago and Bisiaux were dropped from the break before the end of the steep early section of the climb, leaving Omrzel and Berrade to lead the race into the final 12.5km. Omrzel was soon on his own, leaving Berrade behind with 11.7km to go.Four minutes down the mountain, it was Mas who decided to go solo, the red jersey once again attacking his GC rivals after winning stage 9 at the Alto de Aitana. The Spaniard leapt away to a half-minute lead before linking up with García Pierna 9km from the top.The pair held the chase behind at 40 seconds before García Pierna's work was done, 5km from the top. Further back, Tuckwell and Bisiaux had dropped back to help Gall and Roglič, while Carapaz and another Decathlon man, Mühlberger, caught back on.Despite having more numbers than the solo Mas, the chase group made few inroads into the Spaniard's lead. That initial 30-second gap remained, regardless of what was going on behind, and he danced towards the line in no danger of being brought back.Gall and Roglič found themselves alone again on the run towards the finish, having dropped Carapaz, but he made his way back to the duo before the finish, and the three men crossed the line having shed another 27 seconds to the GC leader.Omrzel had already long finished his ride, celebrating a major breakthrough victory two weeks into the first Grand Tour of his career.

item.title: Disastrously-timed puncture sees Filippo Ganna caught out in GC-ending split at Tour of Britain
item.content:encoded: Filippo Ganna saw his general classification hopes at the Tour of Britain go up in smoke on stage 2, as the Italian suffered a mechanical problem just as the peloton was splitting in the crosswinds. Despite the early crosswinds passing by without incident, the race suddenly came to life with 60km to go on Thursday's flat stage to Skegness, and the peloton split in two. Just as the two groups were splitting, Ganna, second overall after his runner-up finish on stage 1, appeared off the back of the race with his arm in the air, appealing for assistance for what looked to be a puncture.Former racer Geraint Thomas, who retired at last year's Tour of Britain and is now Netcompany-Ineos' Director of Racing, scrambled from the passenger seat of the team car to help. As a mechanic grabbed a new bike from the roof rack, Thomas delivered the push-off to get Ganna back up to speed. The damage, however, was done, and Ganna was left scrambling in group of around 50 riders, which quickly found itself almost a minute down on the main pack of 40, where the key sprinters and GC riders were all located. With the exception of their sprinter, Sam Welsford, Netcompany-Ineos put their whole squad in the second group to chase, with some assistance on hand from the Flanders-Baloise team. However, despite moving to within 30 seconds of the lead group with 35km to go, by which point they were in sight, the gap never closed. In fact, from there it only yawned out again amid the merciless pace-setting in the lead group, where the sprint teams, along with UAE Team Emirates-XRG – who don't have a sprinter but several GC cards – all rode hard and in unison. By 10km to go, the gap was back out to one minute and the cause was lost. Ganna eventually crossed the line in 67th place, 1:43 down on the front of the race. He drops to 10th overall, 1:53 down on the leader Lewis Askey (NSN Cycling)In a race that's expected to be decided by tight margins, with stage 4 the toughest day of the race but still light on climbing, Ganna had been considered among the possible contenders. And he'd made a strong start, powering up Michaelgate in Lincoln to place second on a stage that saw small gaps. Stage 1 winner) Askey remains in the overall lead, with UAE possessing a strong hand with Tim Wellens in second at 12 seconds.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Eric Plunk
item.author: Jonathan Farrar
item.content:encoded: Trivia nights are a fun activity at local bars, breweries, and restaurants. The best part of trivia is confidently knowing the answer once it is asked. If you ever find yourself faced with the question, “Who is the only Major League Baseball player to be traded for the same Hall of Famer twice in their career?” the answer is former Yankee Eric Plunk. Another trivia tidbit: Plunk is not the reason behind the phrase or term “plunk,” meaning to hit a batter. No, that is simply a fun coincidence, as the term was coined well before Plunk was born or started throwing baseballs. September 3, 1963 (Wilmington, CA) 1989-1991Plunk grew up in California and attended Bellflower High School. He was drafted by the Yankees in the 4th round of the 1981 MLB June Amateur Draft. The 6-foot-5 right-handed pitcher had a plus fastball to go along with a good curveball, but scouting reports noted that Plunk would occasionally lose command of his offerings.The Yankees had Plunk report to the Gulf Coast League after being drafted. Plunk went on to make 11 starts that season, most of them before his 18th birthday. In 1982, Plunk stayed in rookie ball, this time playing in the Appalachian League. After getting his feet wet playing professional ball, Plunk played the 1983 and 1984 seasons for the Yankees farm team in Fort Lauderdale. Over those two seasons at Single-A, Plunk posted a 20-22 record over 48 starts with a 2.81 ERA in 301.1 innings and had established himself as one of the Yankees’ top prospects.Everything changed for Plunk on December 5, 1984. On that day, he was traded by the New York Yankees with Tim Birtsas, Jay Howell, Stan Javier, and José Rijo to the Oakland Athletics for star leadoff man Rickey Henderson, Bert Bradley, and cash.Oakland assigned Plunk to their Double-A affiliate to start the 1985 season. Plunk made 13 starts in Double-A, going 8-2 with a 3.52 ERA. That was good enough to get the call-up to Triple-A Tacoma. Plunk would struggle and have to grind out the rest of the season, going 0-5 with a 5.77 ERA.To start the 1986 season, Plunk was back in Tacoma. After making six starts, Plunk received his first call-up to the major leagues. Plunk made his debut against Toronto on May 12. Plunk stuck on the roster and finished the season with the Athletics, logging 120.1 innings, making 15 starts and appearing in 11 more games as a reliever.After the season, the Athletics decided they wanted to see what Plunk could be as a reliever. He started the 1987 season back in Tacoma, but was called back up after tossing 34.2 innings with a 1.56 ERA out of the pen, picking up 9 saves in less than a month. Over the rest of the 1987 season in the show, Plunk appeared in 32 games, 11 of which were starts. His final line was 4-6 with a 4.47 ERA and two saves in 95 innings.Heading into the 1988 season, the Athletics decided to use Plunk as one of the primary set-up men for Hall of Famer Dennis Eckersley. In 1988, Plunk threw 78 innings, all out of the pen, and posted a 3.00 ERA to go along with a 7-2 record. The Athletics made the playoffs after winning the AL West, eventually losing to the Dodgers in the World Series. Plunk worked 2.0 clean innings in the 1988 playoffs.In 1989, Plunk would make history. After a solid start to the season, on June 21, he was traded from Oakland along with Greg Cadaret and Luis Polonia to the New York Yankees for Rickey Henderson. This was the first and only time to date that a player was traded for the same Hall of Famer twice. The Athletics, with Henderson, would go on to win the World Series in the Battle of the Bay. Plunk, coming full circle back to the team that drafted him, went 7-5 with a 3.69 ERA in pinstripes in 20 relief appearances and 7 starts. The Yankees would finish the season in 5th place in the division.The Bombers would move Plunk back into his full-time relief role for the 1990 season. Plunk tossed 72.2 innings in 47 games. His ERA was 2.72. The team, however, was not good at all. Posting a record of 67–95, it was the Yankees’ first last-place finish since 1966 and the first last-place in the division era. 95 losses is the most ever by the Yankees, as the 103 losses in 1908 were by the Highlanders.Plunk was with the Yankees for all of the 1991 season. The team was better, but still not very good. Despite being such a strong reliever, the Yankees decided to use Plunk for spot starts in addition to relieving. Plunk’s ERA went up more than 2 full runs, and he was released by the Yankees following the season.Prior to the 1992 season, Plunk signed with the Blue Jays but was cut after spring training. He then landed in Cleveland. The Land is where Plunk would spend the next seven seasons. Just like when he arrived in Oakland, Plunk found himself on another team that was on the verge of making a few World Series runs. In another fun piece of trivia Plunk was the first pitcher to win a game at Jacobs Field. Across those seven years in Cleveland, Plunk pitched 462.0 innings, all in relief. His record was 36-33 with a 3.25 ERA, and he picked up 26 saves — though he never pitched particularly well in October (7.53 ERA in 15 games).In July of 1998, Plunk was traded by Cleveland to the Milwaukee Brewers for Doug Jones. Plunk pitched the rest of 1998 and the 1999 seasons for the Brewers. In 107 innings, he posted a 4.63 ERA and went 5-6. Plunk tried to play the 2000 season but appeared in 7 games for the Cubs’ Double-A affiliate before hanging up his spikes.Over a 14-year career, Plunk went 72-58 with a 3.82 ERA. In total, at the major league level, he threw 1,151.0 innings and pitched in two World Series. He was hurt for Cleveland’s 1995 loss, but his teams could not pull off the win in either.After his playing days ended, Plunk remained attached to baseball. Back in California, he started coaching and working privately with players looking to further their development at The Institute of Sports & Education in Corona, CA.See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

item.title: What's next for Aston Martin's and Honda's F1 development
item.author: Jack Cozens
item.content:encoded: Aston Martin's major Hungarian Grand Prix upgrade package and subsequent refinements it introduced at the Dutch GP look set to be its final developments of the 2026 Formula 1 season.Here are the main takeaways from that - as well as more on what engine partner Honda can do over the remainder of the year.Aston Martin overhauled its car significantly at the Hungaroring before the summer break with the introduction of what essentially amounted to a B-spec car.That 16-part upgrade package included a new, lighter chassis and a new front wing concept - adjustments to which were made after the summer break at Zandvoort, where Aston Martin also introduced revised floor fences and a modification to its diffuser winglet.As a result, the team has introduced the joint-fourth-highest total of updates in 2026, with 34, though it jumps to second on the list - behind only Ferrari - when only performance updates are taken into account. The Race estimates it as being the highest upgrade spender so far this year.Cardile stated, though, that the parts introduced recently would be "the last planned aero developments" for its 2026 car.He said the only exception would be as a result of Aston Martin discovering something in its 2027 car development that "makes sense to test on track this year to help our correlation"."But as of now, nothing more is scheduled," Cardile added.Where more laptime can be foundWhat will still change in the coming month is the weight of the car.Cardile confirmed Aston Martin still had "our weight‑saving programme to complete" and that it expects this to be done at the Azerbaijan GP, from which point "we'll essentially be running the final version of the car for the rest of the season".While there has been no official word on how much Aston Martin is, or was, over the limit, the suggestion is that at its peak the initial version of the AMR26 was 10-15kg too heavy.Cardile said Aston Martin would be "very, very close" to the weight limit by the time of the Baku race weekend on September 24-26."It depends on what you choose as your reference race, but it’s a significant number - enough to dramatically improve laptime," he said, when asked how much weight had been saved."That's a major achievement. Sometimes it comes from changing individual parts. Other times, it means rethinking how something was engineered in the first place - even the chassis. It's a mix of small details and big structural ideas."Cardile said in reference to Aston Martin's recent uptick in performance that he had recognised the frustration felt by drivers Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll and said it was "important for us to get closer to giving them a car they can drive the way they want".Having accomplished that - with Alonso scoring points for only the second time in 2026 with a season's-best ninth at Zandvoort - Cardile said: "Now though, a lot of the conversation with them is about looking ahead. We're asking: what are the limitations of the 2026 car, and how do we make sure we take another big step for 2027?"But while saying the focus for the remainder of the campaign will be to use everything it can learn to "guide the 2027 project", he said there was no expectation that parts from this season would be used next year."Every single part will be new," he said. "Everything will have been improved."But conceptually, it will be an evolution of the direction we took with this year's car."We're on the right path now, but we’re not tied to it. Let's put it this way: when it comes to tackling the '27 project, we haven't placed any constraints on ourselves in terms of trying to carry anything over from the previous car."In this sense, it will be a completely new car, and it gives us the freedom and mindset to achieve what we want."Honda brought its spec 2 engine upgrade to the Dutch GP - and this was an improvement. "We've made a double step, if you like: a big increase in raw performance and a big improvement in driveability," Cardile said.He said at the Italian GP that another countermeasure to improve this would be introduced following work at Honda's Sakura facility.But these kinds of updates are likely to be the extent of what Honda brings over the remainder of 2026.Asked at Zandvoort whether any further hardware improvements were expected for this year, Orihara said: "This is the only major update for this year."But if we found something, a good solution to improve our performance by small modification, that can be on the table. But [there won't be] a major update before 2027."Orihara nevertheless felt there was more power to be found - an estimate is that the Zandvoort upgrade provided a step in the 10-30bhp range - from optimisation."We have brought some calibration change for this track to maximise our performance, but it's going to be no big change, just optimisation," Orihara said at Monza, when asked by The Race whether more performance was available. Alonso said the Honda upgrade was "not a big improvement, to be honest" - as he and Stroll were having difficulty exploiting the extra power - but asked by The Race if he still believed Honda could get back to the title-winning level it was at with Red Bull, he said: "100% yes. 100%."It's a huge commitment from Honda. The facilities we have in Japan are one of the best. I think the personnel and the management of the power unit now has been reinforced as Honda said - and all the people that were in the previous project, they are in again on this one, so I think I have no doubts and I trust 100% Honda."We just need to shortcut somehow that process."

item.title: Scott goes against the racing grain with new Addict Gravel bike, reducing stiffness and adding comfort instead
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: Scott has launched a new version of the Addict gravel bike today, and unlike some of the recent gravel bike launches such as the Ridley Kanzo Fast, it isn't a bike that prioritises all-out speed and aero performance. Instead, Scott seems to have prioritised comfort and user-friendliness. Perhaps the brand foresees a turning point where aero gravel bikes simply become too much for regular riders.The last Addict gravel arrived in 2021, and a lot has changed in the gravel world in that time. The new Addict, as you might expect, has gained boosted tyre clearance, but the brand says the bike is "designed around what matters most: comfort that lasts, stable handling on varied surfaces, and the versatility to carry what you need."There's up-to-date 57mm tyre clearance, a big increase over the old 45mm number, which a lot of best gravel bikes are getting now. Revised geometry, frame layup options, a new gravel-specific cockpit and some neat tool and bag options. The race-oriented 'RC' version of the Addict Gravel will also be discontinued going forward. The brand told us the frame stiffness development of the new Addict Gravel builds directly on the work done for the recently launched Addict and Addict RC road models. Scott claims front-end compliance has been increased by 30% for the new bike. The fork leg design, smaller fork steerer and a new handlebar all contribute to this. Compliance means comfort, and more comfort on off-road terrain should reduce fatigue and help riders go faster. At the back, compliance is said to be up by 60%; the seat tube has been shortened, which means more seatpost to flex and improve comfort. The brand also says the dropped seat stays flexing also helps here. Geometry has also changed to improve comfort and handling across the seven available sizes. The stack is 10mm higher, and reach is 10mm longer. This is offset by a 10mm shorter reach in the cockpit or handlebar. The BB is lower, and the fork rake has been increased, in part to accommodate the larger tyre clearance. The front centre is now longer, placing more front wheel out in front of the rider. Chainstay length is the same as the previous generation bike. In the name of comfort, overall stiffness has been reduced by less than 5% to improve traction and compliance, according to Scott. The brand stresses that the ride will still be precise and efficient but with a more forgiving ride quality.A new gravel cockpit has also been developed for the bike. The bar has an increased forward sweep that the brand says will improve wrist clearance. Reach has been reduced, as mentioned, and the bar has a 'neutral shifter position'; this means that due to the shape of the bar, the brake levers will remain in line with the drops themselves, not sitting out at an angle due to the bar's flare, which the brand says will provide more control. Scott appears to have implemented some handy features and accesories into the Addict Gravel. Like a lot of Canyon bikes now, the majority of adjustments can be made with one T25 Torx key. Tools have also been integrated into either side of the bar drops. One side houses a tubeless repair kit, whilst the other contains the T25 Torx key needed to make hardware adjustments. There's also downtube storage, and the brand's 'Save the day' toolkit contains a tube, levers and a mini pump. There's also a dedicated top tube storage bag to provide additional space for gels, etc. Mounts on the inside of each fork leg also allow for additional water bottle storage if needed.Finally, small parts from the Addict range are cross-compatible compatable opening up more cockpit and stem options and no doubt just generally making life simpler for users.Prices, builds and weights The new Addict Gravel range will consist of five models and ten colourways, along with two frame layup options: the premium HMX carbon fibre and HMF version. Scott lists a weight of 794 grams for an Addict HMX frame and a 990-gram weight for the HMF. Full bike weights start at 7.8kg for the Gravel Premium bike, and rise upto 8.7kg for the Gravel 40 model. Models ascend in order from the Gravel 40 model, through 30,20, and 10 models before topping out at the Premium model. Shimano and SRAM builds are available.Prices start at $3499.99 / £2,499 / €2699 for the Gravel 40 bike and rise to $10,499 / £7,999 / €8,999 for the Premium.

item.title: DT Swiss partners with Wahoo to launch proprietary Trackr Speed hub sensor
item.content:encoded: Most of us use some sort of GPS based device when out on the bike, and most of us have experienced signal dropouts, whether they be in steep-sided valleys, tunnels or densely wooded areas. Even if your device is picking up your heart rate and power, if your device loses sight of the satellites, large chunks of your ride can go missing.To remedy this, Swiss wheel manufacturer DT Swiss has partnered with Wahoo to release its own hub based speed sensor, the Trackr Speed.Designed to ensure your ride is recorded wherever you ride, the DT Swiss Trackr Speed by Wahoo - to give it its full moniker - is designed to clip around the brand's SPLINE and DICUT hubs. Fully encompassing the hub housing, it looks like an integrated part, not an add on and also works with the company’s recently launched 1800 series wheels, ensuring it works with the majority of the gravel and road range of wheels. Using both ANT+ and Bluetooth, the hub connects to your phone, bike computer or smartwatch, and though we’ve not yet had our hands on the Trackr Hub, DT Swiss assures us it’s quick and easy to connect to your device, and more importantly, install on your rear wheel hub. The device uses its own internal battery, the company claiming up to 94 hours life, when it can be recharged in situ using the magnetic charger."When the mountains swallow your signal or tunnels block your connection, this sleek rear‑hub‑optimized sidekick keeps counting," the company’s press release reads, rather poetically. "In partnership with Wahoo, we’ve built a speed sensor that translates every wheel rotation into pure accuracy, even where satellites tap out. No drops. No excuses."According to DT Swiss’s press material, the Trackr Hub uses a "3-axis accelerometer" to measure each rotation of your wheel to accurately measure your speed, though obviously not your precise location. So, while your ride may still appear as a straight line on Strava, at least you’ll know how far you travelled and how fast you were going when the GPS signal was lost, and, in conjunction with power and heart rate data, you’ll know every inch of your ride. You can buy the DT Swiss Trackr Speed either on its own or as part of a bundle with the company’s G1800 SPLINE rear wheel. The device on its own will set you back $89.80 (€59.90 / £54.99), while the wheel bundle will cost you $427.90 (€280.90), with no UK pricing available.It’s certainly a good looking bit of kit and will integrate perfectly with your DT Swiss wheels, and if you ride only their wheels or have a speed sensor for each wheel set you own, its certainly the most elegant and best looking speed sensor we’ve seen.There is a but. Not only is Wahoo’s own speed sensor called the Trackr Speed - formerly known as the 'Wahoo RPM Speed' - it’s waterproof to the same level, uses the same accelerometer technology, works with all wheel brands and looks like it’s easier to swap between bikes, it’s even 10g lighter. It also retails at £29.99, it just doesn’t look as neatly integrated.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Mets take two of three from the Rays
item.author: Peter Brody
item.content:encoded: The Mets did their crosstown rivals a huge solid taking two out of three from the Rays, meaning the Yankees closed the gap to 3.5 games with their extra-innings win over the Angels. Cam Schlittler authored another dominant start and Austin Wells supplied the game winner to ensure the team enters the off-day on a positive swell of emotion before heading to San Diego for three.Here’s how the rest of the games involving the AL playoff picture shook out: New York Mets (63-77) 10, Tampa Bay Rays (83-56) 4Neither team’s starting pitching plans went according to script. Griffin Jax was only able to give the Rays 2.2 innings in his first start off the IL, allowing six runs (three earned) on seven hits and two walks. The Mets meanwhile tried to get cute with a bullpen game, only to watch opener Justin Hagenman and reliever Chris Devenski combine to give up four runs on six hits and a walk in 3.2 innings. New York scored the first six runs of this contest, starting with three in the first. Juan Soto singled and Carson Benge walked to set up a two-run single from Jared Young aided by a missed catch error by the catcher on a play at the plate. Marcus Semien then drove in Young with a double. Two innings later, they scored another three runs. Bo Bichette singled, Semien walked, and A.J. Ewing singled to load the bases with two outs. A Brett Baty double promptly unloaded them to make it 6-0. Tampa Bay responded with four unanswered, starting with one in the third as Taylor Walls walked, Yandy Díaz singled, and Jonathan Aranda plated Walls with a single. Three more came the following inning, Chandler Simpson and Cedric Mullins reaching on singles to set up a three-run blast to right by Richie Palacios.Then it was the Mets’ turn to score four unanswered. Three of those arrived in the seventh as Bichette doubled, Benge singled, and Semien was hit by a pitch to load the bases. They received their second bases-clearing double of the night, this one courtesy of rookie Nick Morabito, his first ever big league hit. Soto demolished a solo shot in the eighth to push the Mets into double digits. Seattle Mariners (66-74) 8, Boston Red Sox (75-65) 3Bryce Miller was pulled after just 65 pitches despite no report of an injury — a curious decision given he had held the Red Sox to a run in 4.2 innings to that point. It was even more curious considering the Mariners had spotted hima 4-0 lead with a long rally in the third. Weston Wilson and J.P. Crawford hit a pair of leadoff singles and Dominic Canzone walked, Julio Rodríguez and Josh Naylor then following with their own back-to-back singles as Seattle plated four with the help of a wild pitch and a Jarren Duran throwing error.The lone damage against Miller came in the fourth on a Trevor Story RBI double. However, Seattle responded with another four-run inning in the sixth. Cole Young got plunked, Wilson walked, and Crawford singled to load the bases with no outs. Jhonny Pereda singled home a pair, Randy Arozarena another, and a Canzone double made it 8-1.Roman Anthony grabbed a consolation run with a solo home run in the seventh and Mickey Gasper and Eli White added another with back-to-back doubles, but that would conclude the scoring. With the loss and Yankees win, the Red Sox fall five games back of second place.Houston Astros (71-69) 2, Chicago White Sox (73-66) 3We had a true pitchers’ duel on our hands, Davis Martin giving the White Sox 5.2 scoreless allowing five hits and a walk while Hayden Wesneski was even better for the Astros — seven scoreless innings of one-hit ball with two walks and five strikeouts. Houston had the first real chance to score, with runners on the corners with no outs after Yordan Alvarez led off the fourth with a double and Isaac Paredes followed with a single, but Martin buckled down to strand them in place.Chicago squandered a golden opportunity in the eighth after Tristan Peters led off with a triple and Drew Romo drew a walk to put runners on the corners with nobody out. However, Peters got thrown out at home on a groundball. Munetaka Murakami singled to load the bases, but Miguel Vargas killed the rally with the inning ending double play.Houston capitalized in the bottom of the frame, Alvarez singling, Paredes walking, and Jose Altuve getting grazed by a pitch to load the bases with one out. Nelson Velázquez supplied the game winning hit with a two-run single off Sean Newcomb.Toronto Blue Jays (69-71) 11, Cleveland Guardians (70-69) 0The Blue Jays bludgeoned Joey Cantillo for nine runs (four earned) in 5.1 innings. Those five unearned runs all came in the second when a throwing error by shortstop Angel Genao allowed two runs to score. The very next batter was Vladimir Guerrero Jr., and he completed the humiliation with a booming three-run blast. Dylan Cease kept pace with Schlittler in the AL Cy Young race, twirling six shutout allowing four hits and no walks with four strikeouts. Vladito would collect another pair of RBIs late and finish with three hits in this rout of the Guardians.Colorado Rockies (54-86) 6, Baltimore Orioles (69-71) 5Luis Robert Jr. drove in a pair on his Orioles debut while Trevor Rogers struck out eleven across 6.2 innings of two-run ball. However, the Rockies kept chipping away until a Zac Veen RBI double with two outs in the bottom of the ninth sent the game to extras. In the 11th, Samuel Basallo and Blaze Alexander slapped a pair of RBI singles, but Colorado walked it off by scoring three in the bottom half on TJ Rumfield RBI single, Adael Amador ground-rule double, and the walk-off two-run single by Brett Sullivan. Athletics (54-86) 9, Texas Rangers (69-71) 2It was a home run parade for the Athletics in Arlington, four different players leaving the yard. Rookie Nick Bolte became the first player in franchise history to hit two home runs and steal a base from the leadoff spot as he went 3-for-4 with four RBIs. Zack Gelof and Jonah Heim both hit solo shots while Alika Williams provided pop from the bottom of the order with a two-run blast and an RBI double. This was all after Texas jumped out to an early 2-0 lead on solo homers by Ezequiel Duran and Justin Foscue.

item.title: 'Waking up at 5am to go race our bikes – that's easy' – Megan Guarnier picks up where she left off in Philadelphia Cycling Classic
item.author: laura@cyclingnews.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: For Megan Guarnier, holding a top position in the peloton while powering up the 16% gradients of the Manayunk Wall five times in the Philadelphia Cycling Classic was the easy part. She had already spent the last five years scaling a mountain of loss and grief while raising two young boys."Momming to two boys is a full-time, exhausting position! So actually coming to a bike race like this is a bit of a vacation," Guarnier tells after the race."Waking up at 5:00 a.m. to go race our bikes – that's easy!"Ten years ago, Guarnier was on top of the cycling world, having won prestigious events like the Giro d'Italia and Tour of California. She landed podiums in La Flèche Wallonne and Trofeo Alfredo Binda, narrowly missing one in the Tour of Flanders, and was the first overall winner of the UCI Women's WorldTour.She was the US national champion and represented her country in the Olympic Games. And, of course, she won a somewhat different edition of the Philly Classic, too. At each step, her husband Billy Crane was her biggest supporter. She credited him for convincing her to quit her day job and pursue cycling full time.In 2018, Guarnier announced she was going to retire, go back to school and start a family. She planned to keep a toe in the sport as a mentor for the Tibco women's team. However, those ambitions fell away when Crane was diagnosed with terminal cancer."Yeah, so directly after I retired, we welcomed my little boy. And directly when he was born, my husband was diagnosed terminal," Guarnier tells after finishing 10th in the Philadelphia Cycling Classic."We only got about a year with him after that. So there was the grief process, and then we had my second little boy."Cancer took Crane in May of 2021, leaving Guarnier to raise her son Ned and his little brother Theodore while navigating the unimaginable. Eventually, her old rim-brake bike became a vehicle for finding a way through it."My friend got me back out on the bike. I wasn't riding at all through that whole process, just staying fit," Guarnier said. "I got back out on the bike and found another part of myself that I had been missing for quite a bit of time."Soon, Guarnier was back in the sport, working with the CCB Kenetik women's development team."Then when [team manager] Tim [Mitchell] called me up and asked me to work for the team, I was like, 'I don't know, Tim, I haven't been in bike racing, haven't really been on bikes'," she explained.Even so, her knowledge and deep insights proved to be valuable for the young team. She planned to be in the team car for Philly and not on the start line, but having just been with them for their training camp in Spain, Guarnier decided to fill an open spot on the team."The spot opened up, and I'm like, Tim's in the car, and I'm a little bit extra in the car, so why not get on the bike if I can help them?", she said."I can help them be a little more insightful - just the mentality of how to tackle each lap. Because I've done it, I know how it feels, and I know where the important points are and how to mentally handle that."Sometimes [it's better] being able to directly show them on the bike - because the car is in the caravan, in the back, and they don't really know what's happening."Guarnier showed no signs that she's been away from competition for the better part of eight years, and was right near the front on the first ascent of the Manayunk Wall - the very place she won the last edition of this race."A lot has changed!" she said when asked how it felt to be back. "The equipment's changed – everybody makes fun of me for my rim brakes! It's of a different era, as am I."It was super fun. The crowds out there were unbelievable," Guarnier said. "I was really excited to see how much this has grown. All along the course, there were people going up the Wall. Just the energy out there was awesome. And it wasn't even the finish line this year. So to have that many people on all of the hills, yeah, it was a lot of fun."Whether or not the thrill was enough for Guarnier to come out of retirement and race full time remains to be seen."One day at a time!" she says. "Being a mom of the best two little boys and having this opportunity to work with this team, again, it's all about having fun and passing my knowledge on to these girls. Because that's the goal with CCB, is to develop these women so they can be the future of the world for the US."I'm really excited with the whole thing - we were talking about the ebbs and flows of a race. Somebody says, 'Oh, I'm not feeling good,' and then how you change their mindset so they can feel better, or just focus directly on the next thing that's coming."So it's just been a fun process and kind of finding myself again after all the loss and all the change."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Tour of Britain Men: Tim Merlier outpaces Olav Kooij to win stage 2 reduced bunch sprint finish
item.content:encoded: Tim Merlier (FixAll-QuickStep) sprinted to victory on stage 2 of the Tour of Britain, on a chaotic day that saw the peloton split in two some 60km from the finish.Sprinting from a vastly reduced bunch of 30-odd riders, the Belgian kicked convincingly clear of Olav Kooij (Decathlon CMA CGM), with Sam Bennett (Pinarello-Q36.5) clinching the final spot on the podium.Stage 1 winner Lewis Askey (NSN Cycling) finished safely in the peloton to retain the green jersey as the overall leader of the race.Thursday’s 180km journey from Boston to Skegness, with just two very minor climbs on the menu, was always likely to end in a sprint finish, and Merlier was the hot favourite of those fast finishers. However, it was far from a straightforward stage as crosswinds blew in from the North Sea.The wind didn’t cause a problem during the early part of the stage, despite teams riding in echelon formation. Alertness was high, but the pace was low, and there were no splits to speak of as they rode calmly behind the day’s four-man breakaway.However, that all changed 60km from the finish, when the pace picked up and the peloton suddenly split in two. For Filippo Ganna (Netcompany Ineos), the split came at the worst possible moment, as the Italian suffered a puncture and had to stop for a bike change.Ganna and his Ineos teammates would spend the rest of the race chasing in the second peloton. For a while, it looked like he would return as, with help from Flanders-Baloise, the gap came down from one minute to less than 30 seconds, with the group ahead in sight at several moments.However, they couldn’t close the gap, and from 30km out it started to drift back out again, reaching the minute mark once more with just over 10km to go.At that point, it was a lost cause. There had been no shortage of interest up front in driving on the move, with QuickStep, Decathlon, Tudor, and notably UAE all pulling hard in the first peloton. UAE don’t have a sprinter here, but for a second day in a row they sent Florian Vermeersch on a late attack, the Belgian soloing from 7km out and surviving until 2km to go.QuickStep did the lion’s share in bringing him back, and it was Jasper Stuyven who led out the sprint for the Belgian team. Merlier was nowhere near his wheel going into the final 500 metres, but after coming out of the late left-hand bend, he jumped early from far back, with around 200 metres to go, and stormed to the front.From there, no one could get near him, and Kooij had to settle for second place fully in the slipstream.In the overall standings, Askey leads by 12 seconds over UAE’s Tim Wellens, who replaces Ganna, who has now tumbled out of overall contention. Matteo Trentin (Tudor), who bagged bonus seconds at the second intermediate sprint, moves up to third at 19 seconds.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Nvidia buys Hugging Face, the GitHub of AI, for $13 billion
item.author: Michael Acton, Financial Times
item.content:encoded: Nvidia has agreed to buy AI model platform Hugging Face for $13 billion, in the latest step by the $5.4 trillion chip giant to use its financial might to accelerate the technology’s boom while exerting greater control over the industry.Hugging Face, which only last year turned down a large investment from Nvidia at a $7 billion valuation to maintain its independence, serves as a repository for millions of models and data sets and has become a champion of “open” AI systems.Nvidia said the goal of the deal was to speed up the spread of open models. Unlike proprietary models from labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic, the design of open-weight models is public and users can download, customize and run them on their own hardware.

item.title: 'I want to win more races no matter what they are' – Lennert Van Eetvelt switches Lotto for NSN in three-year deal
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Van Eetvelt joins after racing for Lotto-Intermarché for the past four seasons, having come up through Lotto's development ranks.During his time as a pro, Van Eetvelt's standout results have included wins at the 2024 UAE Tour and Tour of Guangxi. He also has a podium at the 2024 Donostia San Sebastián Klasikoa to his name, as well as top-10 results at the Volta Catalunya, Strade Bianche, and Il Lombardia."Lennert Van Eetvelt is a rider we have followed closely over the past years, and we’re very pleased to welcome him to the team," said NSN general manager Kjell Carlström."Lennert has already demonstrated his ability to win at WorldTour level, particularly in demanding stage races, and we believe he can continue to develop over the coming seasons with us."After a strong 2024 campaign, Van Eetvelt's progress has seemed to stall in the past two seasons. The 25-year-old hasn't won a race since Guangxi two years ago, left his Tour de France debut last year following a crash, and made little impact on this year's race after going into it with a rib injury.Results have been more positive recently, however, with Van Eetvelt racing to second overall at the Arctic Race of Norway. He's set to take on the GPs de Québec and Montréal and Il Lombardia before the year is out.“What stands out is not only his climbing ability, but also the way he races. He is willing to take opportunities when they present themselves and has shown that he can finish off races against strong competition," Carlström said."Whether it's targeting the GC in stage races, the Ardennes classics, or showing what he can do in the mountains in Grand Tours, we are excited to see what Lennert can do in NSN colours."Having raced on junior squads in Belgium before joining the Lotto setup, Van Eetvelt said he's now looking forward to working in an international team for the first time."I was looking for an international and professional environment to take the next step in my career. NSN felt like the perfect fit for that, so I'm really looking forward to joining the team and seeing what we can do together over the next three years."I want to win more races no matter what they are. I know what my capabilities are, and I want to build the strongest palmarès I can from them, so I hope to hit the ground running in 2027. I'm confident I have made the right choice, and together, we will win races."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors
item.author: Donna Lu
item.content:encoded: Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizesMemory is an imperfect thing: research shows that recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ from those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence.“What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney.Continue reading...

item.title: The plastic waste overtaking New York – and the people trying to curb it
item.author: Photo essay by Bryan Anselm, words by Dharna Noor
item.content:encoded: From New York to Quebec, photographer Bryan Anselm spent months capturing spaces overrun with plastic and the actions individuals and groups are taking to reduce wasteIn New York City, the plastic we discard has a way of remaining in plain sight. There are few alleys to hide residents’ refuse, and the clear recycling bags leave their contents on full display. In a city built on a dense grid, lightweight wrappers, bags and bottles spill from overflowing bins and skitter down sidewalks, collecting in gutters and corners before the wind carries them on.All that plastic is a layer of the urban landscape, as familiar as subway grates and fire escapes, revealing a messy and unflattering aspect of city life. “Garbage is not what we cast out, but the prime locus of meaning in our lives,” the character Nick Shay says in Don DeLillo’s Underworld.Continue reading...

item.title: The Yankees’ top defensive plays of August
item.author: Sam Chapman
item.content:encoded: Another month of Yankees baseball is in the books, and though their situation in the American League East has changed little of late, there was plenty of good baseball to take in. With each passing game comes more moments to remember and appreciate, including those made by Yankee defenders. August was no different, as we saw plenty of web gems in the Bronx this month, so let’s take a look back at some of the best from the last month. August 4: Lombard’s slick play starts a double playWhile the defensive slump George Lombard Jr. found himself for part of August is likely the lasting memory, the month also brought plenty of highlight reel plays. Here, early in the month against the Cardinals, the rookie backhanded a sharp two hopper before throwing across his body to kick off an inning-ending double play. Despite the low points of late, we should be seeing highlights at short from Lombard Jr. for years to come.August 5: The rookie fully extends up the middleSpeaking of which, why not take a look at another gem from Lombard Jr.? Here, just a day after our first featured play, the Yankees shortstop dove to stop a one-hopper destined for center field. Lombard Jr., after fully extending, quickly got up and threw a seed over to first base, just barely nabbing St. Louis’ JJ Wetherholt. The bad sticks out this month, but there was a of good to soak in from Lombard Jr. in August. August 7: García Jr. fully over the shoulderAnother play from the first week of August, this time with Luis García Jr.’s range on display. With the go-ahead run on third base in the tenth inning for Atlanta, the Yankees first baseman was in a full sprint straight backwards, only to reach over his shoulder and snag the would-be blooper. Not exactly known for his defense, García Jr.’s clutch play saved the game in extras, putting an end to the Braves’ half of the inning. Even sweeter, it was a game the Yankees would eventually win in the bottom half of the inning.August 18: Austin Wells slides in foul territoryAnyone with experience donning the gear can attest to how difficult a pop up can be from the catching position. Here, Austin Wells makes a difficult one look pretty straightforward. Jackson Holliday lofted a ball toward the third base dugout into foul territory. Immediately set on his intention, Wells ran full speed to the warning track, calling for the ball the entire time, before sliding on a knee to secure the out for his club. Sometimes, making the tough ones look easy can be a highlight on its own. August 28: Bellinger preserves the lead with his armPerhaps more than almost anyone else, Cody Bellinger is a regular on these monthly lists. Toward the end of the month, Belli changed things up, this time making the cut with an exceptional play not with the glove, but with his arm. With the Yankees holding just a 1-0 lead in the seventh, Bellinger caught a relatively shallow fly ball, before perfectly timing his crow hop, and delivering a one-hop strike to home plate. His perfect throw nabbed the runner at home, and preserved what would remain an important 1-0 win for the Yankees at home against the Red Sox.

He is the latest face of Armani Beauty, with the brand saying Carlos represents “authentic elegance, fierce discipline” - and we have to agree. Carlos looked the part, too, during his latest visit to Venice, attending the Venice Film Festival, just before heading to Monza for the Italian GP this weekend. Giorgio Armani dressed a group of their guests for opening night, including Sainz. He wore a Giorgio Armani tuxedo, which included an ivory dinner jacket, standing out among the sea of black tuxedos, and paired it with black trousers. item.title: A2RL's international racing debut: What you need to know
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: The most advanced autonomous racing series in the world has headed to Europe for the first time, with Imola hosting a race between five autonomous single-seaters this Saturday.The Abu Dhabi Autonomous Racing League (A2RL) returns with its first major on-track event since staging its 2025 finale in Abu Dhabi last November, where teams competed for a $2.25million prize pool.This time around, five teams have qualified for a race at Imola this Saturday, where they'll race Super Formula cars which have been heavily adapted to drive autonomously.Here's everything you need to know about A2RL's international debut:Teams are using the A2RL EAV-25 platform, which marks a huge step forward from the series' initial autonomous concept.There's no better evidence for that than it lapping just 1.58 seconds off ex-F1 driver Daniil Kvyat at Abu Dhabi last November, having been 10 seconds adrift at Suzuka just 18 months prior to that."Still, today, after two and a half years here, I'm still amazed when I see this car running," A2RL technical director Nicola Palarchi told The Race at Imola."The level of performance when they approach, when they attack a corner is amazing."And thinking that there's no one there [in the cockpit], and it's not remote control...there's no predefined driving or strategies, the car is driving by itself and making its own decision, [is] mind-blowing."Imola presents a huge, new challenge for the technology, with far more bumps and kerbs than Abu Dhabi, very little margin for error with gravel traps aplenty, and variable weather conditions.So teams have been given nine days of testing at Imola prior to the Saturday finale. They all have identical EAV-25s and the autonomous stack that sits within the cockpit and has been developed by the series, but it's down to the teams to code their AI machines to be the fastest.Teams qualified their cars at the end of those nine days of testing, with Italian outfit Unimore Racing coming out on top, ahead of fellow home team Polimove. 1m37.314s +1.084s +1.746s +2.936s +3.964sSeason one and two champion TUM was third, but it knows the result is far from settled.That's because these autonomous cars really can race each other, with TUM passing Unimore for victory in the Abu Dhabi finale last year.Just like in traditional motorsport, there are also trade-offs for the teams to make when programming the cars, in terms of one-lap speed and race pace, so there's every possibility that the order will change in Saturday's race.The laptimes have been very competitive too. A2RL says the fastest time got to within eight and a half tenths of the benchmark human laptime, set by current Super Formula driver Juju Noda.The cars have been weatherproofedPresently, the weather forecast is for a scorchingly hot and dry Saturday at Imola. But should that change, A2RL is now ready for it.A2RL's testing at Suzuka in 2024 exposed one vulnerability with the initial cars: in wet conditions, the sensors and autonomous stack were exposed to moisture, which caused some issues.Therefore, a rainproofing kit can be fitted to the EAV-25, which means it can run in the wet - and has done successfully - at Imola. It even ran in hail conditions.That kit includes sharkfin louvres on the cockpit to cover air exhaust vents, cockpit cover seals, and specifically designed and engineered rubber 3D-printed camera sleeves to seal the forward camera hatches."We are very happy; we have been working on a rain kit for some time," Palarchi told The Race."We had some rain already in 2024 when we were preparing for the exhibition in Suzuka at the time of the Super Formula event."We have been focusing on this in the last few months, as we knew we were coming to Imola and the weather is not as stable as in Abu Dhabi."So we managed to roll out the rain kit that was very successful, and the teams could enjoy wet track condition, which was a first also for all of them."The five-car race will take place on Saturday, September 5 at 6.30pm local time.

item.title: Fem van Empel says she's 'happier than ever' amid cycling career break
item.content:encoded: Fem van Empel has stated that she is "happier than ever," eight months into her career break from cycling. She has kept a low profile away from the sport since then but offered a glimpse into the reset it has provided with a social media update on Thursday, to mark her 24th birthday. "Little me would be so proud,' Van Empel wrote alongside a photo of herself as a child."Grateful where I stand today: healthier and happier then ever!! Cheers to 24 years."There is no indication at this point if Van Empel has any plans to return to cycling, but the latest post would indicate that the bold career pause has been very beneficial. Van Empel's troubles first emerged early in 2025, when, after winning her third straight cyclo-cross world title, she rode just two Classics on the road before announcing a mid-season break as the "best step for my mental health and well-being". She returned to action in September and planned to race a full cyclo-cross season, but by mid-December she had taken the decision to take an indefinite break from the sport. "This is a well-considered decision that I feel good about. At the moment, both the motivation and the enjoyment I have had in cycling for years are missing," Van Empel said at the time."I wanted to be honest and fair about this with the team. For now, this is the best choice. It feels like the right time for a new chapter. I am very grateful for all the support I have received from the team, my family, and the fans, and I look forward to what the future brings."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Florian Lipowitz returns to racing seven weeks on from Tour de France-ending crash – here's what's left of his season
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Seven weeks on from his Tour de France-ending crash, Florian Lipowitz is making his racing return, the German racer heading to the late-season Italian Classics to end his 2026 season.Lipowitz, along with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe co-leader Remco Evenepoel, was in contention for the Tour podium when he crashed during the stage 16 time trial in Thonon-les-Bains. He suffered a broken collarbone in the fall, which meant he left the race from fifth overall.On Wednesday, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe announced that the 25-year-old would make his return to the peloton at the Giro della Toscana on September 9."More than anything, I'm looking forward to pinning on a race number again and racing. After seven weeks without competition, I can't know exactly where I stand," Lipowitz said."That's what we want to find out. For me, these first races aren't about results. I want to see how my body responds to the demands of racing, get back into the rhythm and then decide together with the team what is still possible this season."Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe noted the race is part of a performance assessment ahead of the final weeks of the season.He's tentatively penned in for several more races, but participation will depend on how Toscana goes. The race is "less about achieving a result and more about establishing where Florian stands ahead of the remaining weeks of the season," the team said.If all goes well, Lipowitz should race on to the Coppa Sabatini (September 10), the Memorial Marco Pantani (September 12), and the Trofeo Matteotti (September 13)."When returning from an injury, the goal is not to get back to your previous training load as quickly as possible. We have to build load tolerance and performance in parallel," said team director of coaching, John Wakefield."With Florian, we saw early on that we were making good progress and that we could at least consider the originally planned return to racing a realistic goal. But the key is to assess every step based on how he responds to the load – not based on a date in the calendar."Lipowitz still has almost a week of training before returning to the peloton, but he's already thinking of bigger goals further ahead."Of course, the World Championships are a race that appeals to me. But one thing is also clear: if my form isn't good enough, I don't want to take a spot away from another rider," he said."We have a lot of strong German riders who are well suited to the course in Montréal. I want to wait for these first races and take an honest look at where I stand. If the form is there, I'd really like to race the Worlds – but I'm not putting any pressure on myself about that right now."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Italian GP tipped for mad 'MotoGP-style' race with F1 2026 cars
item.author: Jon Noble
item.content:encoded: Formula 1 figures are bracing for the potential of a particularly wild Italian Grand Prix weekend at Monza, as slipstream is expected to massively impact both qualifying and the race.Aston Martin trackside chief Mike Krack has forecast "a record of all times" in terms of overtaking in the grand prix, while 22-car Q1 - due to the massive benefit of towing and complexities of energy strategies - is particularly at risk of being dominated by the efforts to catch a slipstream.F1 is heading to one of the most challenging venues for the new turbo hybrid 2026 cars, with Monza's long straights meaning cars are going to run out of battery energy easily.Cars struggling for top speed on the straights, allied to the new active aero characteristics of straight and corner mode, means that there is now a much bigger benefit than there has been in recent years from receiving a tow.Being in the slipstream of the car ahead will not only help increase top speed marginally by reducing drag, but will also deliver gains in terms of battery deployment - as less energy will need to be burned to push the car through the air.Williams chief engineer Paul Williams reckons that slipstreaming could become a "significant tactic" once more. And Krack went as far as to express hope the gains do not trigger a repeat of what happened at Monza in 2019, when drivers tripped over themselves trying to get a slipstream at the end of qualifying.Asked by The Race if slipstream games were back in play at Monza this year, having fallen away in recent years, Krack said: "I think yes!"I think the lack of energy that you have here over the qualifying lap will manifest itself in people looking for that."I hope we will not have a situation like 2019, certainly not in Q1 - but who knows what will happen? Nobody wants to be first probably, but I think there will be more of this than we have seen here recently."Cadillac driver Sergio Perez said of slipstreaming at Monza: "In previous generations it was [already] very critical. "Now it's going to become even more, with the lack of energy that we're going to experience. "We saw already in Spa it was around two seconds to a second and a half, so I think it's going to be really close. "It's going to be a bit messy [in qualifying] because everyone will be trying to get some towing."Measures are in place in modern F1 after the chaos of 2019 that should mitigate the issue, as the FIA has instituted a minimum laptime delta - but it's exceedingly rare for this to lead to a driver penalty, and the FIA may have to be stricter with enforcement this year than is convention.One question that will only be answered when cars are running together is whether excessive slipstreaming could prompt some safety concerns.This could become an issue if there are wildly different deployment strategies in play that mean there are big speed differentials between cars in areas of the track.Krack said: "Normally if you see the deployment profiles, they converge over a weekend - so I do not expect any major differences. "But if people deploy completely differently, then there is always a risk."F1 teams know that this weekend is going to be incredibly challenging from an energy management perspective and that some unusual tactics may need to come out.Krack felt that the new rules will force a completely different approach for teams."Monza is a bit of a new game this year that we need to learn how to handle," he said."I think all the teams will have to learn and maybe what we know about Monza is not necessarily true anymore."One of the main uncertainties for qualifying will be how best to unleash energy coming out of the final Alboreto or Parabolica corner for the start of a qualifying lap.Teams will have to work out where the best place is to go on full power to maximise speed for the start of the lap, but without burning up so much battery that they run short before the first chicane.Despite the FIA's measures to combat these issues of energy starvation, Perez said: "You're going to get into this situation where if you went half a percent too much in one corner on throttle, it's going to cost you even a few tenths. "Belgium [Spa-Francorchamps] was very critical in that regard and I expect that here it's going to be, like, the worst of them all."Krack suggested Monza could produce an extreme level of yo-yo racing.He said it remained unclear how easy overtaking would be, but expected it will "probably will be a record of all times here, or like MotoGP".Though Monza's layout should naturally lead itself to this kind of racing, that hasn't really been the case in F1 in recent years - with the venue struggling to deliver much in the way of wheel-to-wheel action, though Formula 2 and Formula 3 have remained "overtake-fests".This time, the expectation is of a grand prix more in line with those kinds of categories."Top speeds are way down from the past - which is a bit of a shame, but on certain straights you can make a bigger difference than before when it comes to defending or attacking," said Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas."It's been normally a good place for racing anyway but now it adds another element of more dynamic racing here. So no doubt there's going to be plenty of overtakes."Rookie Arvid Lindblad was more pessimistic, though, after what he described as "the most confusing sim session of the year" in preparation for Monza's unique energy challenges."I think the first two laps will be interesting, depending where you spend your energy you'll pass three cars and then lose to three cars," he said. "[After that] I don't know if there's going to be much passing. "I think the difference to other tracks, even energy-starved ones, if you use the boost it takes you one lap to recover, so you're a bit slow on the next two or three straights, but one lap after you're alright, whereas here it takes a lot longer to recover. So basically if you use the boost, you gain on one straight, but then you're so slow for the next three laps. "So I think it will... you could call it 'yo-yo racing' maybe, but I just think it will be really bad yo-yo racing. Even in the past it used to be decent, we would actually be passing each other, whereas now it's just, you're going to pass the guy and then you're just going to lose a second and a half. I don't know what to expect, but I'm not very optimistic."

item.title: UK homeowners: has the hot weather damaged your property?
item.author: Guardian community team
item.content:encoded: Are you dealing with subsidence or other issues caused by the hot weather? During a dry spell, such as the successive heatwaves that affected some parts of the UK this year, houses built on clay-rich soil suffer as moisture is sucked away by trees and bushes. This causes the clay to shrink and foundations to drop, causing structural problems.We would like to speak to homeowners who are dealing with damage to their homes which is likely to have been caused by this year’s extremely hot, dry weather.Continue reading...

He's after green jersey points mainly, but he's also close enough to the lead of the mountains jersey that that could be of interest to him too...He's not going to win that jersey but it would be nice to wear it.September 3, 2026 – 7:26 AMJay Vine gave a kind of avoidant interview to Eurosport. Saying he's not feeling good, but he doesn't know why. He didn't want to say much.September 3, 2026 – 7:29 AMVine is struggling at the back, whilst his teammate Oliveira is off the front with a couple of riders. Still not an established break as we approach the top of the climb.September 3, 2026 – 7:31 AMPlenty of riders have been in the action today.September 3, 2026 – 7:32 AMGregor Muhlberger (Decathlon CMA CGM) stopped and got off his bike, and also started taking his shoe off. Not sure if he's needing a bike change or a shoe change...September 3, 2026 – 7:32 AMUp front, Eddie Dunbar (Pinarello Q36.5) is leading the way in trying to get into the break, but nothing is sticking yet.September 3, 2026 – 7:34 AMWout van Aert wins maximum points with a little sprint over the top.September 3, 2026 – 7:34 AMVan Aert and Buitrago have just chipped off the front of the peloton with that KOM effort.September 3, 2026 – 7:38 AM20km done, Van Aert and Buitrago are reeled in. The breakaway battle starts anew.September 3, 2026 – 7:39 AMVan Aert isn't having a bad Vuelta, but his own team admitted that he does need to win for himself at some point. Today is probably too hard, but it's still good to see him in the mix.Return to lead-out duties for Wout van Aert brings Visma more success at Vuelta a España, but he also needs wins himself says DS'Hopefully he will win one stage, but on the other hand, he is an excellent teammate, and he wants to help Matthew Brennan win more stages' says Frans MaassenSeptember 3, 2026 – 7:41 AMA new move has a pretty decent gap.Alexey Lutsenko (NSN), Axel Laurance (Netcompany Ineos) and Ramses Debruyne (Alpecin-Premier Tech).September 3, 2026 – 7:41 AMYoung Aussie Hamish McKenzie (Jayco AlUla) has quit after crashing yesterday.September 3, 2026 – 7:42 AMThe three leaders have a bigger gap that anyone has had today, but I'm not sure three is a big enough break for today. I would say too many teams will be chasing behind for this to be able to stick.September 3, 2026 – 7:49 AMWe've got just over 20km of rolling road now before the next categorised climb.Various riders are trying to chase across to our three leaders.September 3, 2026 – 7:55 AMOscar Onley looks to have come off heavily round a roundabout, his white jersey is covered in dirt from the road. He's remounted his bike and he's chasing back on.Luke Tuckwell also went down, and a rider from Picnic PostNL.September 3, 2026 – 7:55 AMNo teammates with Onley just yet. He's just drafting behind the Ineos car.September 3, 2026 – 7:56 AMOof just saw the replay of the crash. Onley just slid out on the exit of the roundabout, landing on a patch of grass outside a Lidl. Looked heavy by the grass will have softened the blow.September 3, 2026 – 7:57 AMThe Scot got a nice word of encouragement and a push from his former Picnic teammate Timo Roosen.September 3, 2026 – 7:58 AMOnley and fellow chasers are a minute down on the peloton because the bunch are going at full pelt now. They'll be able to get back on but it's not ideal.September 3, 2026 – 7:59 AMAmazing landscapes in Andalucía.September 3, 2026 – 8:00 AMBack to the front of the race, our three leaders have just been joined by a large group of chasers – over 20 of them. Big group at the front now.September 3, 2026 – 8:00 AMThe gap is still small. Teams will have to asses who has made it and who hasn't before they decide if this big move is going to be allowed to go.September 3, 2026 – 8:02 AMVan Aert is in this 27-rider front group. But I think they're about to be caught and the situation will reset once again...September 3, 2026 – 8:06 AMSeems I spoke prematurely – the peloton is slowing up so I think this break of 27 will be our move of the day.I'll list the full names when we have them.September 3, 2026 – 8:06 AMOscar Onley is back in the peloton, so Ineos can relax briefly now.September 3, 2026 – 8:07 AMThe peloton are going almost comically slow now, letting the gap go out to a minute.September 3, 2026 – 8:08 AMSome riders in this break don't seem to want to be in such a big group. A few of them are trying to get away in a smaller break.September 3, 2026 – 8:09 AMOscar Onley is visiting the medical car.Check the widget above for a list of names in the break.September 3, 2026 – 8:12 AMHere's the names in the break:September 3, 2026 – 8:13 AMThe biggest GC threat in the group is Jakob Omrzel (Bahrain Victorious) who sits at 8:05 down on Enric Mas, so Movistar will have to keep this somewhat controlled.The gap is approaching three minutes currently. September 3, 2026 – 8:13 AMPretty impressive to see Tuckwell in this break after crashing today. He crashed last weekend too.September 3, 2026 – 8:20 AMMovistar are on the front of the bunch.September 3, 2026 – 8:22 AMThere is a chasing group in between the peloton and the break – it's made up of Pavel Sivakov (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), Chris Hamilton (Picnic PostNL) and José Manuel Díaz (Burgos Burpellet BH). They're about a minute behind the break.September 3, 2026 – 8:26 AMDíaz and Hamilton have joined the break. Sivakov hasn't made it. Should be 30 riders in the lead now.September 3, 2026 – 8:27 AMCorrection, Sivakov has made it, so 31 in the lead. Tracker is showing him as behind but we can see he is in the break.September 3, 2026 – 8:30 AMVan Aert wins maximum points again. He really is keen to go after this jersey, but he's only made up 2 points in his 11-point deficit to Buitrago.September 3, 2026 – 8:32 AMHere's a look at Wout van Aert in the break.Who do you think will win today? Break or peloton? Let me know in the comments.September 3, 2026 – 8:33 AMImages of Onley's crash, in case you missed it.September 3, 2026 – 8:35 AMSivakov confusion again. It was not him that we could see joining the break... He's actually given up and waited for the peloton. September 3, 2026 – 8:40 AMThe gap has just reached five minutes.September 3, 2026 – 8:43 AMBuitrago is pushing on in the front of the break, trying to whittle things down a bit.Riders like him will be hoping they can get rid of Omrzel, because that will give a smaller break a better chance of winning the stage.Van Aert, Almeida, Lutsenko, Bisiaux and Kron are with him.September 3, 2026 – 8:44 AMStill a lot of action and climbing to come today.September 3, 2026 – 8:48 AMThat early attempt to split up the break hasn't really worked, still a big group all together at the base of this long climb.September 3, 2026 – 8:50 AMBahrain are understandably taking a lot of responsibility in the break. They have KOM points and GC positions to gain.September 3, 2026 – 8:51 AMIf you're looking for something to read whilst the race is relatively calm, I spoke with Paul Seixas yesterday about his upcoming races.Paul Seixas raring to take on Canadian GPs and World Championships with Pogačar possible absence opening up opportunitiesFrench star will return from post-Tour de France break at Grand Prix Québec before big goals of Worlds and Il LombardiaSeptember 3, 2026 – 9:02 AMStill 11km left of this climb to go. It hasn't been too eventful so far.September 3, 2026 – 9:05 AMIt's deceptively calm right now. Still two really big climbs to come after this one.September 3, 2026 – 9:11 AMThe gap is up to six minutes now. How much elastic are the peloton going to give this break? At what point does it come un-closeable?With two such long climbs left, a lot can change in the finale, so six minutes definitely isn't too much to close, but I wonder what Movistar's strategy is here.September 3, 2026 – 9:20 AMWoooops Luke Tuckwell nearly crashed into a soigneur in the feed zone there. Just about avoided disaster.September 3, 2026 – 9:25 AMVan Aert and Buitrago go head to head for the points and WVA wins it again.September 3, 2026 – 9:26 AMVan Aert has 30 points in the KOM classification now, and Buitrago has 38.September 3, 2026 – 9:27 AMVan Aert and Buitrago are on their own on the descent again, just pushing on after that KOM sprint. Some riders are committed and taking their turns but others are not quite sharing the load. These are the two best-placed GC riders in the break.September 3, 2026 – 10:36 AMI think Omrzel is riding for his own interests, but for Bisiaux, his role is more about being a satellite rider for Felix Gall.September 3, 2026 – 10:38 AMCarapaz is still on his mission behind, but it feels a bit futile.He's five minutes behind the break and only 22ish in front of the peloton.September 3, 2026 – 10:38 AMBisiaux declines to work with Omrzel.September 3, 2026 – 10:41 AMOmrzel and Bisiaux have 17 seconds on the next group, but only the Slovenian is working.September 3, 2026 – 10:42 AMCarapaz is caught by the GC group after a big pull from Romeo.September 3, 2026 – 10:42 AMEnjoying our live race coverage?
